abstract: Fibre-linked optical clocks sense tidal changes of the gravitational potential, but separating overlapping tidal components and quantifying their precision remain challenging. Using strontium and ytterbium clocks 692 km apart, we measure over 353 days a response of 0.95 (0.11) to the combined solid-Earth and ocean-loading tide and 1.01 (0.13) for the lunar semidiurnal group, and separate the lunar and solar-frequency semidiurnal contributions. A signal-to-noise model based on the actual sampling accounts for the lunar precision and guides future clock-network observations.
hook: Two optical clocks 692 km apart felt the Moon's tides, matching predictions within about 10 percent.

readout.label: Measured tidal response vs. model, Earth plus ocean

summary: Strontium and ytterbium clocks linked by fibre measured the tidal change in gravitational potential over 353 days. The response to the combined solid-Earth and ocean-loading tide was 0.95 with uncertainty 0.11 relative to the model, and 1.01 for the lunar semidiurnal group. Only one clock pair and one stretch of time were used, so the precision is limited.
title: Tidal potential measured with distant optical clocks
